passage: I'm Arohi. In Class 5, school felt like being scratched all day. The label in my uniform collar poked like a thorn. The tube lights buzzed. The bell rang right above our door, so loud my teeth hurt. By lunch I was snapping at everyone, and then I'd go silent. Francis Sir noticed me holding my ears at the bell. He didn't say I was rude. He asked, "What bothers you most here?" I told him everything. Mummy cut out the labels that night. Francis Sir moved my seat to the window, away from the bell and the buzzing light, and let me wear soft ear covers at bell time. The next week I didn't snap once. I even laughed at recess.

qa.q: Where did Francis Sir move Arohi's seat?
qa.a: To the window, away from the bell and the buzzing light.

qa.q: Why was Arohi snapping at everyone by lunch?
qa.a: The poking label, buzzing lights and loud bell made Arohi feel scratched and worn out all day.

qa.q: What small changes helped Arohi most?
qa.a: Cutting out the labels, a window seat away from the bell and light, and ear covers at bell time.

qa.q: How might Francis Sir's question have felt different to Arohi than a scolding?
qa.a: It showed Arohi that the discomfort was believed, so Arohi could explain instead of feeling blamed for being rude.

grounding: It shows a child who cannot bear labels, lights and the school bell and seems irritable, helped by small changes like a quiet seat and ear covers.

passage: Class 3 teacher's note on Tenzin For two weeks Tenzin has been pale and grumpy after lunch. He sits with his arms folded, head down, and refuses to answer. Some children call him moody. Today I watched closely. In the canteen he covered his nose with his sleeve and ate almost nothing. Under the bright lights in the art room he squinted and put his head on his arms. What I did next: I let Tenzin eat his tiffin in the library corner with one friend, and I turned off the two lights above his table in art. I told his family what I saw. This afternoon he finished his tiffin and painted a mountain with three yaks. - Akash Sir

qa.q: Where does Tenzin now eat his tiffin?
qa.a: In the library corner with one friend.

qa.q: What does Tenzin covering his nose in the canteen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the canteen smell bothered him a lot and made him unable to eat.

qa.q: Which of Akash Sir's steps was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Watching closely before judging; it showed the smell and lights were the problem, so small changes could fix them.

qa.q: How might the children who call Tenzin moody see him if they understood?
qa.a: They might see that he was uncomfortable, not moody, and be kinder when he goes quiet.

grounding: A teacher sees a child who seems withdrawn because of the canteen smell and bright lights, and small changes like a quieter place help a lot.

passage: Class note, Year 4. Tenzin has been snapping at classmates for weeks and pulling at the back of his collar. Today he put his head down, covering his eyes, and said the lights "buzz and sting." I noticed the tube above his desk flickers. I moved him to the seat by the window, where he can work in daylight, and asked his parents if they could cut out the tag in his shirt. At lunch the bell rang and he flinched hard, so I offered him ear defenders for bell times. By afternoon he had finished his worksheet and even laughed with Pema at the next desk. Next: ask maintenance to replace the tube. — Sarika

qa.q: What did Tenzin say about the lights?
qa.a: He said the lights "buzz and sting."

qa.q: How had Tenzin been feeling at school, and how did it show?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and irritable, snapping at classmates, pulling at his collar and hiding his eyes from the lights.

qa.q: Which small changes helped Tenzin?
qa.a: A window seat away from the flickering tube, asking for the shirt tag to be removed and ear defenders at bell times.

qa.q: How might Pema see Tenzin by the afternoon?
qa.a: Pema may see him as friendlier and easier to be with, now that he is laughing instead of snapping.

grounding: Shows a child bothered by tags, bright lights and the bell who seems irritable, and how small changes like a new seat and ear defenders help.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Fish fry day again in the canteen. The smell hit me at the door and my stomach flipped. I pretended I wasn't hungry and sat with my lunchbox closed. Kashish asked why I was being grumpy. I wasn't being grumpy! I just couldn't breathe properly.
Then today the counsellor said I can eat in the library corner with one friend on fish days. Kashish came with me. We ate parathas and talked about her cat, and I actually finished my lunch.
It's not me being fussy. The smell really makes me feel sick. Now I know a small thing can fix it.
Dilnaz

qa.q: Where can Dilnaz eat on fish days now?
qa.a: Dilnaz can eat in the library corner with one friend on fish days.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Kashish called it grumpy?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt misunderstood and upset, because the smell made breathing hard and the stomach flip, not a bad mood.

qa.q: How did the counsellor's plan help?
qa.a: It gave Dilnaz a quiet place away from the smell with a friend, so Dilnaz could eat and not be seen as fussy.

qa.q: How might Kashish understand Dilnaz after eating in the library?
qa.a: Kashish may realise the problem was the canteen smell, not grumpiness, and feel glad to help.

grounding: Shows a child who cannot bear the canteen smell and seems irritable, and how a small change like a quiet place to eat helps.

passage: The village school near Kottayam had no electric bell; the peon struck an iron plate with a rod. Every time, Joseph, nine, dived under his desk. The older boys called him a coward, and one teacher called it drama. Aparna Teacher watched for a week. Then she moved his seat to the far end of the verandah, away from the plate, and let him cover his ears with a folded scarf. On Friday she asked, "Would you like to strike the bell at the last period?" Joseph held the rod, knowing exactly when the sound would come. He struck it three times and grinned.

qa.q: How was the bell rung at the village school?
qa.a: The peon struck an iron plate with a rod.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel each time the bell rang?
qa.a: He felt frightened and overwhelmed by the sudden loud sound, diving under his desk.

qa.q: What did Aparna Teacher do that was wiser than calling it drama?
qa.a: She observed him, moved his seat away from the plate, let him cover his ears and gave him control of the bell.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Joseph after he rang the bell himself?
qa.a: They may stop calling him a coward, seeing him confidently strike the bell and grin.

grounding: Shows a child distressed by the school bell and dismissed as dramatic, and how small changes like a far seat and ear cover help.

passage:
At his primary school in Kraków, Yosef was known as the boy who sulked. He kept pulling at the back of his jumper where the tag scratched. The strip lights buzzed in his eyes. At lunch he ate in the corridor because the canteen smell of cabbage made him gag. When the bell rang, he flinched and snapped at whoever was nearest.
His teacher, Mr Marek, noticed one day that Yosef's shoulders dropped when the lights were off for a film. After class he asked, "Which things bother you most?" Yosef listed them, surprised anyone wanted to know.
The next week Yosef had a seat by the window, far from the bell, and a pair of soft ear defenders in his desk. His mum cut out all the tags. By Friday he laughed in class for the first time that term.

qa.q: Where did Yosef eat lunch?
qa.a: He ate in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when he snapped at people after the bell?
qa.a: He felt jangled and irritable because the noise, lights and smells were genuinely uncomfortable for him.

qa.q: What small changes helped Yosef, and why?
qa.a: A window seat far from the bell, ear defenders and tag-free clothes reduced the discomfort, so he no longer needed to withdraw or snap.

qa.q: How does Mr Marek see Yosef after their talk?
qa.a: He sees that Yosef's sulking came from real discomfort, not a bad attitude, and wants to help.

grounding: Yosef can't bear tags, lights, the canteen smell and the bell and seems irritable and withdrawn, and a quiet seat and ear defenders help.
